parts:
Hi,=20
I am conducting two different surveys; one using pellet counts (quadrates=
)=20
and one using line transect counts of kangaroos in order to compare metho=
d=20
efficiency and accuracy. As part of the line transect design I downloaded=
=20
Distance 5 and have loaded spatial maps of my study site, divided into tw=
o=20
strata (high and low density). Sampling effort was allocated based on den=
sity,=20
with higher sampling in high density site. The location of transect lines=
(x,y)=20
were imputed into the gird later under the data tab.=20

Problem:
At this stage density is being underestimated, which I attributed to how=20=

Distance 5 is currently analysing my data. The problem I think is the use=
of an=20
effective strip width (200m in this case) for density estimation. Where s=
urvey=20
lines are adjacent (within 20m) to different strata, Distance 5 is assumi=
ng a=20
full 200m for which observation could be made. This is not the case as=20=

observations made in different strata to the line are not included in dat=
a, as=20
per instruction in using stratification. Consequently, density is being e=
stimated=20
assuming a much greater area, then what was actually surveyed, leading to=
=20
density underestimation. This is how I understand it.=20

The problem also occurs where transect lines are bordering the end of the=
=20
reserve, say 30m from boundary. At this site no animals occur beyond the=20=

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: stratification
parts:
Brett, I would be very surprised if your interpretation of the problem
is correct. You have just 2 strata. You don't say how many lines per
stratum, but presumably only a small proportion of line falls within one
stratum but just 20m from the other. In any case, even if this
proportion were high, Distance does not assume that you have a larger
stratum area than you do, and there should be little bias. If you
believe edge effects are problematic, there is discussion of these
issues (including the issue of a line hitting a boundary, and the effect
of that) in the 2004 advanced distance sampling book. But unless you
have very odd strata, I doubt that this is the cause of your problem.

If you think Distance is underestimating because you get higher
estimates from the quadrat sampling of pellets, then things to look at
include:

Estimates from pellet surveys correspond to an average density over the
period that pellets persist. If there are movements in or out of the
area during this period, or between day and night, then the estimates
will not be comparable with line transect estimates.

If you use standing crop methods for pellets, you may have a biased
estimate of pellet disappearance rate. See section 6.2 of the 2001
intro to distance sampling book.

If you use clearance plot or standing crop methods, you may have a
biased estimate of defecation rate.

You don't say how you survey the lines - aerial, vehicle or foot. The
assumptions to look out for are: do animals respond to the observer
before they are detected - e.g. by moving away from the line? Do you
detect all animals that are on or very near the line? Do you have an
accurate method (e.g. laser rangefinders) of estimating distances? Can
you accurately estimate cluster (group) sizes?

Steve Buckland

Brett Howland wrote:

> > and one using line transect counts of kangaroos in order to compare method

> > with higher sampling in high density site. The location of transect lines (x,y)

> > were imputed into the gird later under the data tab.
> >

> > Problem:
> > At this stage density is being underestimated, which I attributed to how

> > Distance 5 is currently analysing my data. The problem I think is the use of an
> > effective strip width (200m in this case) for density estimation. Where survey
> > lines are adjacent (within 20m) to different strata, Distance 5 is assuming a
> > full 200m for which observation could be made. This is not the case as

> > observations made in different strata to the line are not included in data, as
> > per instruction in using stratification. Consequently, density is being estimated
> > assuming a much greater area, then what was actually surveyed, leading to

> > density underestimation. This is how I understand it.

> > The problem also occurs where transect lines are bordering the end of the
> > reserve, say 30m from boundary. At this site no animals occur beyond the
> > boundary and therefore the assumption of 200m strip width is again

> > inappropriate. Is there a way for Distance 5 to account for the difference in

messages.author: 6c182657d328642f
messages.subject: Re: stratification
parts:
Hi Steve,
Thanks for the quick reply.
I know the exact number of animals at the reserve, so I am not comparing pellets with line transect, but line transect with true.

To provide a bit more background, the site being surveyed is only small (130ha) and the two strata roughly divide the site in two. I have about 20 lines of variable length, with most located in the high density strata.

Given the small size of the reserve, and the large strip width (200m) I see a problem. For example, suppose I conducted a survey on a single 400m line within a square, with dimensions 400m x 400m, and by chance the line was located along the southern boundary of the square 10m from the edge. No animals occur outside the square so I am essentially only recording animals on one side of the line. When I enter the data into the program however, it assumers I was observing animals on both sides of line within an estimated strip width. Density will be underestimated in this example; compared to if the line had been located in the centre of the square.

If I understand distance correctly the program uses a strip width, multiplied by length of line for basic estimation of area surveyed. This procedure is incorrect in the above example and is incorrect in my survey, where a number of lines are close to a boundary for which animals can not be recorded past.

Cheers,
Brett

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: stratification
parts:
Brett, I suggest you read the chapter on survey design in the advanced
distance sampling book. It deals with edge effects. We also deal with
these issues in

Fewster, R.M., Laake, J.L. and Buckland, S.T. 2005. Line transect
sampling in small and large regions. /Biometrics/ *61*, 856-859.


Contrary to what is said in the response to that article, it is easy to
implement the wrap-around solution, provided you can walk a line in the
bufferzone - see chapters 7 and 10 in the advanced distance sampling book.

You say you have 20 lines, then you give an example with just one line.
If just one line in 20 has this problem, then any bias will be small.
(Not all 20 can run parallel to a boundary, and only 10m from it - at
most 2 could.) Again, I reiterate that the method does NOT assume that
you covered a region larger than the region specified. The only issue
that can cause some bias is that detections fall off more rapidly than
they should, because there are no animals to be detected beyond the
boundary. Even that does not cause the bias you might anticipate,
because the reduction in effective strip width and the reduction in
encounter rate tend to compensate. So while you get a biased estimate
of the detection function, any bias in the density estimate is much
smaller. Incidentally, in your extreme example, you could simply record
one side of the line, and record half the effort for that line - see
pp304-6 of the introductory distance sampling book.

You could get underestimation of density when you have a small study
region and a small number of lines. This can be resolved by good
design. You may need to resort to extending the design into a
bufferzone around the study region. This compensates for the lack of
detections at larger distances, by putting some lines outside the
region, with the observer looking in, to give extra detections at larger
distances. However, given good design, it would be unusual for this to
make a large difference. Therefore in your case, if you believe that
you have a good design, yet the bias is large, I would look at the
assumptions of the method. Is there undetected responsive movement? Is
it possible that animals on or near the line are being missed? Might
distance estimates be biased?

If you still believe it is the design that is generating the bias, then
try sampling into the bufferzone. You might also want to try simulating
the method, if you believe that we have got the method wrong!
Simulations have to be very extreme to break the method, especially if
you have as many as 20 lines in a systematic random design.

Steve
